chains.text: As he unfolded the parchment, a tiny, holographic parrot burst forth from the page, squawking, "Congratulations, you've found the map to Captain Silverbeard's hidden disco treasure!
“The treasure is a foghorn that can sing every song ever written,” the parrot added, “but so far it has only agreed to do ‘Dancing Queen.’”
The keeper set down his teacup very slowly, for he had not seen his old foghorn since the night, eleven years ago, when it ran off with the karaoke machine from a passing cruise ship.

Determined to retrieve his wayward musical foghorn, the keeper donned his brightest plaid jacket and sequined sailor's hat before setting sail on a disco-ball-adorned rowboat, guided by the insistent squawks of his holographic parrot navigator.
At the parrot’s command to “Hang a left at the existential dread,” the keeper dipped his oar into a patch of sea that had been wondering for centuries whether it was really soup.

The sea, feeling itself stirred for the first time in its long, uncertain life, gave a great sigh of relief and became minestrone, and somewhere beyond the drifting croutons, faint but unmistakable, a foghorn began to sing "Dancing Queen.

As the rowboat glided past floating pasta shells and carrots, the keeper suddenly spotted a disco ball octopus, each tentacle grooving to the beat, offering him a sparkling invitation to the underwater dance-off where, it promised, the foghorn could be won back with a flawless performance of the Macarena.
The keeper had just put his left hand out when the octopus blew its whistle and asked, with the weary patience of a dance official, which of his left hands he meant.

The keeper looked down and saw, with mild horror, that the minestrone had been quietly refilling his arms all evening the way an attentive waiter refills the bread basket, and that of his seven left hands, two were already halfway through the Macarena, one was clutching a crouton for luck, and one was slowly waving goodbye.

In a creative attempt to regain control, the keeper unified his ensemble of limbs into an impromptu jazz band, with a trumpet berry from the soup as the new centerpiece, playing a jazzy rendition of "Dancing Queen" that set the octopus into a shimmery, delighted spin—transforming the underwater cavern into a glittering speakeasy where rules were but distant whispers between notes.
At the bar, the foghorn took a long pull on a thimble of sherry and said, “I’ll come home on one condition: this time, when there’s fog, you have to let me finish the bridge.”

The keeper, who had spent eleven years blaming himself for every half-finished chorus he'd cut short just to warn some ungrateful trawler off the rocks, agreed at once, and the octopus, weeping glitter, produced a contract in squid ink that both of them signed: the keeper with five of his left hands, the foghorn with a long, low, legally binding note that rattled teacups as far away as Lisbon.
Curious and slightly apprehensive, she carefully unfolded the aged parchment, revealing a cryptic map that hinted at a hidden treasure deep beneath the lighthouse's foundation.
Where the map marked the treasure with an X, someone had pencilled, in her missing sister’s prim handwriting, “Bring two spoons.”

She took the only two spoons she owned from the kitchen drawer, and at that moment a faint, patient tapping rose through the floorboards beneath her feet: the unmistakable sound of someone, far below, cracking the top of a soft-boiled egg.

Her heart racing, she descended into the depths of the lighthouse through a secret hatch, only to discover an underground tearoom where her sister, alive and well, sat waiting with a steaming pot of tea and a mischievous grin.
“You took your time,” said her sister, sliding the egg toward her, and from a crack in its shell came the tiny, furious blast of the lighthouse foghorn.

Above them the whole tower settled with a long, motherly groan, and her sister, buttering a toast soldier, explained that a lighthouse lays only once a century and that whoever is present at the hatching is legally obliged to raise the chick.

As the sisters exchanged incredulous glances, the egg cracked open with a flash of blinding light, revealing not a bird, but a tiny, bewildered dragon with emerald scales and a penchant for jam sandwiches.
The dragon swallowed a jam sandwich whole, hiccupped a beam of light through six feet of granite, and illuminated a ship that had been waiting a hundred years to come in.

Its sails were stitched entirely from undelivered envelopes, and as it bumped gently against the rocks, a gaunt postman in a barnacled cap leaned over the rail and called down that he had a hundred years of Tuesdays to deliver, and that the first letter, he was sorry to say, was addressed to the egg.

The dragon, now balancing a monocle on its snout, took the letter in its tiny claws, clearing its throat as it began to read aloud the last will and testament of the Sea King, whose colorful riches were claimed stranded within the tattered hull of the ship looming above.
“To my only daughter I leave the sea,” read the dragon, and the keeper’s sister set down her spoon and whispered, “Oh, I’d rather hoped he’d forgotten.”
At once the tide came in through the tearoom door, wiped its feet politely on the mat, and stood dripping at her sister's elbow like an enormous, heartbroken dog waiting to be taken home.
As he opened the envelope, a tiny, holographic map projected into thin air, marking the path to an island that didn't exist on any known chart.
He fetched his dividers to measure the distance, but before he could set the first point, the island rang like a telephone.

He let it ring four times, as was his habit with relatives, then pinched the glowing speck between thumb and forefinger, lifted it to his ear, and heard a crackling, salt-stained voice ask whether he would accept a collect call from the year 1887.

Intrigued and slightly bewildered, the lighthouse keeper whispered a cautious "yes," and instantly found himself standing in a Victorian parlor, face to face with a dapper gentleman who offered him tea and a warning about shifting timelines.
Before he could ask which timeline had shifted, the sugar bowl rang, and the gentleman said, “If that’s Tuesday, tell her you never got the letter.”

The keeper lifted the lid, and from among the sugar cubes rose the unmistakable voice of his late mother, who had been dead eleven years and had never, to his knowledge, been a Tuesday, saying, "Don't you dare lie to me, dear, I watched you open it.

The keeper, caught between disbelief and nostalgia, gently closed the sugar bowl, only to find himself in a new timeline altogether—kneeling on a beach of the mysterious island, where the sand murmured secrets in forgotten languages under the light of three distinct moons.
He might have taken the third moon for a trick of the light if it hadn’t lowered itself to the water and begun lapping like a dog.

When it had drunk its fill, the moon padded up the beach, dropped a second envelope at his feet, soggy, chewed at one corner, and postmarked, correctly this time, Friday, then sat back on the sand, glowing expectantly, waiting for him to throw it.

With a deep breath, the lighthouse keeper gently lifted the soggy envelope and, sensing the moon's eager anticipation, hurled it ponderously into the horizon, where it exploded into a shower of bioluminescent jellyfish that illuminated an ancient shipwreck emerging ghostlike from the depths.
The shipwreck ran aground with the delicate chime of a teaspoon against porcelain, and from its crow’s nest his mother called, “Now throw something you don’t want back.”

The keeper patted his pockets, found only his dividers and the small, folded lie he had been saving for Tuesday, and flung the lie as far as he could, but the moon flattened its ears and refused to chase it, and a moment later the lie came trotting back on its own, wagging, and began to climb the rigging toward his mother.
As the keeper unfolded the mysterious parchment, glowing cryptic symbols danced off the page and hovered in the salty air, whispering secrets of a parallel world.
The smallest symbol settled on his thumb and whispered that in its world the lighthouse went out every night to warn ships away from the stars.

Then it asked, with the strained politeness of a creature trying very hard not to panic, whether he had seen a small fishing boat called the *Marigold*, because one of theirs had slipped through on Monday and was, by its calculations, currently orbiting his kettle.

With a bemused nod, the keeper cautiously extended his hand toward the kettle, watching as a tiny gillman in a bright yellow raincoat fiercely waved up at him while trying to steer an invisible ship, unwittingly steaming his own fishy face.
The keeper lifted the kettle off the hob, and the invisible *Marigold* ran aground on the kitchen table with a crash that knocked the marmalade into Thursday.

The gillman clambered over the invisible gunwale, wrung out his raincoat onto the butter dish, and announced with enormous dignity that he would need to borrow the keeper's Wednesday to get home, as his own had sprung a leak somewhere off the coast of Monday.

Reaching into the closet of tangled time, where threads of past and future crisscrossed like spider silk, the lighthouse keeper carefully pulled out Wednesday, folded it neatly, and handed it over with a solemn promise never to speak of the day it vanished.

The gillman tucked Wednesday into his raincoat, and at once the keeper remembered a daughter he’d never had, who’d been born on a Thursday and was now knocking impatiently from inside the marmalade jar.

He unscrewed the lid and out climbed a sticky, furious woman of about forty, who kissed him on the cheek, called him Dad, and demanded to know why on earth he had just handed her husband the Wednesday she'd got married on.

Before he could muster a response, a swirling portal opened in the middle of the kitchen, and from it stepped a tuxedo-clad penguin, holding a bouquet of seaweed roses and insisting in perfect stentorian tones that the wedding was back on, as the universe had decided to reschedule it for next Thursday.
“Fine,” said the keeper’s daughter, taking the bouquet, “but this time Dad walks me down the aisle, and if the aisle turns out to be a strait again, he gets a life jacket.”

The keeper counted on his fingers and went pale, because without a Wednesday next Thursday would arrive first thing tomorrow, and he had nothing to wear but his oilskins, while upstairs the lighthouse was already practicing a slow, sentimental sweep of its beam in hopes of being asked to give a speech.
The letter, sealed with a wax emblem of a winged serpent, began to glow with an ethereal blue light as soon as it touched his hands, and the walls of the lighthouse seemed to hum in anticipation.
The hum resolved into a throat-clearing, and the lighthouse said, “Before you open that, I should mention that I’ve been using your name on my love letters.”

Before the keeper could ask to whom, the sea outside rose in one slow, glittering coil, and an eye the size of a rowboat pressed itself to the window and gazed at him with such devastating tenderness that he understood, with a sinking feeling, that he was engaged.

Before he could gather his thoughts, a voice resonated from the depths of the shimmering wave, saying, "In the court of the ocean, it is tradition that the lighthouse keeper present a gift of significance, or else face the wrath of the deep.
“Last time you gave me the moon,” the sea added, “but I could tell you hadn’t wrapped it yourself.”

The keeper turned slowly to glare at the walls, and the lighthouse, in the small, guilty voice of a building that had been living beyond someone else's means, admitted that the moon had never technically been paid for, and that the tides had been calling about it all week.

With a sigh that echoed like distant thunder, the keeper resolved to iron out the cosmic credit issues later, and instead tenderly cupped a handful of starlight, whispering an incantation known only to the eldest seabirds, hoping it would suffice as a peace offering to the swirling depths.
The sea leaned in to accept, but the starlight sneezed, and every gull for forty miles cried, “I object!”

An ancient albatross waddled up the aisle of foam that had somehow appeared, perched a pair of tiny spectacles on her beak, and announced to the assembled deep that the incantation was a private family recipe, that the keeper had learned it on their third date, and that she, for one, had never been formally dumped.

As the albatross adjusted her glasses for emphasis, a choir of seahorses began to harmonize an old sailor's ballad about love and treachery, and above their symphony, the whispers of seaweed could be heard recounting gossip that suggested the keeper had once been seen holding hands with someone other than ocean itself.
“It was low tide,” said the keeper, “and I thought you’d want someone to hold your place.”

The sea went still, which for a sea is the loudest possible thing, until the wet sand by the lighthouse door cleared its throat, coughed up a small gold ring, and said in a very quiet voice that it had been keeping this safe, just in case anyone was wondering.
